units.title: Climate and energy

words.def: coming from a natural source that will not run out, such as the sun or the wind
words.ex: Wind and solar power are ___ sources of energy.

words.def: a fuel such as coal, oil or gas, formed over millions of years from dead plants and animals
words.ex: Coal is a ___ that formed from plants millions of years ago.

words.def: gases that are sent into the air, for example by cars and factories
words.ex: The city wants to cut its carbon ___ by half.

words.def: the amount of carbon dioxide that a person's activities add to the air
words.ex: Cycling instead of going by car reduces your ___.

words.def: able to continue for a long time without harming the planet
words.ex: Bamboo is a ___ material because it grows back very quickly.

words.def: to use energy, fuel, food or time
words.ex: Old fridges ___ much more electricity than new ones.

words.def: working well without wasting energy, time or money
words.ex: LED bulbs are more ___ than old bulbs because they waste less energy as heat.

words.def: a long period with little or no rain
words.ex: After months of ___, the river was almost dry.

words.def: a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly down a mountain or valley
words.ex: As the planet warms, the ___ is shrinking a little every year.

words.def: to produce energy, such as electricity or heat
words.ex: Wind turbines ___ electricity when the wind blows.

words.def: affecting or including the whole world
words.ex: Plastic in the oceans is a ___ problem, not just a local one.

words.def: a strong effect that something has on something else
words.ex: Cars have a big ___ on the air quality in cities.

words.def: material that stops heat from escaping, for example from a house
words.ex: Thick ___ in the roof keeps the house warm in winter.

words.def: to use as little of something as possible, so that it lasts longer
words.ex: We can ___ water by taking shorter showers.

words.def: a gas, such as carbon dioxide, that traps heat in the air around the Earth
words.ex: Methane, which is produced by cows, is a powerful ___.

words.def: very great or very severe; much more than usual
words.ex: Scientists expect more ___ weather, such as heatwaves and floods.

words.def: the average height of the surface of the sea
words.ex: As the ice melts, the ___ around the world is slowly rising.

words.def: something that you can choose instead of something else
words.ex: Cycling is a cheap and healthy ___ to driving.

words.def: to take in a liquid, a gas or heat, like a sponge takes in water
words.ex: Dark clothes ___ more heat from the sun than white ones.

words.def: a flat piece of equipment that turns sunlight into electricity
words.ex: A small ___ on the roof of the shed powers the lights in our garden.

grammar.q: Hundreds of new wind turbines ___ in the North Sea in recent years.
grammar.why: The turbines didn't build anything, so use the passive. 'In recent years' goes with the present perfect: have been built.

grammar.q: Next year, solar panels ___ on the roof of every new house in our town.
grammar.why: This is the future passive: will be + past participle. The panels don't install anything themselves.

grammar.q: Plastic bottles can ___ into new clothes.
grammar.why: After a modal verb like 'can', the passive is be + past participle: can be recycled.

grammar.q: If we ___ the lights off last night, we would have saved energy.
grammar.why: Third conditional (an imaginary past): if + had + past participle, then would have + past participle.

grammar.q: I wish our school ___ solar panels on its roof.
grammar.why: When we wish the present were different, we use a past form after 'wish': I wish it had...

grammar.q: ___ the rain, the solar panels still produced some electricity.
grammar.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun (the rain). 'Although' needs a full clause, such as 'Although it rained'.

grammar.q: We're going to ___ our loft insulated before the winter.
grammar.why: 'Have something done' means you pay someone else to do the job: we're going to have the loft insulated.

grammar.q: The lights are still on in the empty classroom. Someone ___ forgotten to switch them off.
grammar.why: 'Must have' + past participle shows we are almost sure about the past because of the evidence.

grammar.q: The Sun, ___ is about 150 million kilometres away, gives the Earth almost all of its energy.
grammar.why: Use 'which' for a thing in a non-defining clause (between commas). 'That' is not used after a comma.

grammar.q: A new solar farm ___ near our village at the moment.
grammar.why: The work is happening now and the farm doesn't build itself, so use the present continuous passive: is being built.

sentences: Wind turbines have been built along the coast of Scotland.
If only the bus ran on electricity.
Have you ever calculated the size of your carbon footprint?
More houses are being fitted with solar panels.
Forests absorb huge amounts of carbon dioxide from the air.
A new solar farm is being built near our village.

reading.title: An island powered by the wind
reading.text:
Samsø is a small Danish island with about 4,000 residents. In the 1990s, it depended on oil and on electricity from coal power stations on the mainland. Today, it is famous around the world as an island that produces all of its electricity from renewable sources.

The change began in 1997, when Samsø won a national competition to become a renewable energy island. However, the plan could not succeed without local support, and at first many islanders were worried. Would wind turbines spoil their beautiful views? Would the project cost too much? Rather than forcing the idea on people, the organisers held meetings in village halls and listened to their concerns.

The key decision was to let local people own the turbines. Farmers, families and businesses bought shares, so the money from the electricity stayed on the island. As a result, the turbines became something to be proud of rather than something to complain about.

Within about ten years, Samsø's turbines were generating more electricity than the island needed, and the extra power was sold to the mainland. Many homes are now warmed by local heating stations that burn straw, a waste product from farms.

Samsø shows that the biggest challenge in changing how we use energy is not always the technology. Often, it is persuading people to work together.

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: to show how a community worked together to change its energy
to explain how a wind turbine works
to persuade readers to move to Samsø
to compare the costs of oil and coal

qs.q: Everyone on Samsø supported the project from the very beginning.
Islanders themselves own some of the wind turbines.
Electricity on Samsø is now cheaper than anywhere else in Denmark.
What is used to heat many homes on Samsø today?

reading.title: Reading the past in ice
reading.text:
In the middle of Antarctica, it is so cold that the snow which falls each year never melts. Instead, each new layer presses down on the layers below and slowly turns them into solid ice. Over a very long time, this ice has built up into a sheet that is more than three kilometres thick in places.

As the snow is squeezed into ice, tiny bubbles of air are trapped inside it. These bubbles are like miniature time capsules. To study them, scientists drill deep into the ice sheet and pull out long cylinders of ice, known as ice cores. The deeper the ice, the older it is, and some cores contain air from more than 800,000 years ago.

By analysing the bubbles, researchers can measure how much carbon dioxide there was in the atmosphere in the distant past. Other clues in the ice allow them to work out what the temperature was like. Their results show that, over long periods, carbon dioxide levels and temperatures have risen and fallen together.

The ice cores also reveal that there is more carbon dioxide in the air today than at any time in at least the last 800,000 years. This is one of the clearest pieces of evidence that burning fossil fuels is changing the Earth's climate.

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: to explain how ice can tell us about the Earth's climate in the past
to describe what it is like to live in Antarctica
to persuade readers to visit the South Pole
to explain why snow never melts

qs.q: The ice at the bottom of a core is younger than the ice near the top.
Scientists can study ancient air that is trapped in the ice.
Drilling a deep ice core takes several years.
What have scientists learnt about carbon dioxide and temperature?
opts: Over long periods, they have risen and fallen together.
Neither of them has ever changed.
Temperature has no link with carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide only rises in winter.

extra.q: Everyone can ___ a difference by using less energy at home.
extra.why: 'Make a difference' is a fixed phrase that means to have a good effect.

extra.q: The country's energy ___ fell last year. (consume)
extra.why: We need a noun for the amount used: consumption. A 'consumer' is a person who buys or uses things.

extra.q: Solar power is clean and cheap. ___, solar panels produce no electricity at night.
extra.why: 'However' introduces a contrast: first a good point, then a problem.

extra.q: Which sentence is the most suitable for an academic essay?
opts: Burning fossil fuels significantly increases carbon emissions.
Burning coal and stuff is really bad for the air.
Loads of carbon gets pumped out when we burn things.
Fossil fuels? Seriously bad news for the planet!
extra.why: Academic writing uses precise words (significantly, emissions) and avoids chatty phrases like 'and stuff' or 'loads of'.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'Electricity from the sun is getting cheaper'?
opts: The cost of solar power is falling.
Solar power is becoming more expensive.
The sun produces less electricity than before.
Most cheap electricity comes from the sun.
extra.why: 'Electricity from the sun' is solar power, and 'getting cheaper' means the cost is falling.

extra.q: Which sentence best continues the text? 'Many countries are building wind farms out at sea. ___'
opts: This is because winds are usually stronger and steadier over the ocean.
However, wind is a type of weather.
For example, sea water is very salty.
As a result, people enjoy swimming in summer.
extra.why: 'This is because' gives the reason for the idea in the sentence before it.

extra.q: If we keep using oil at this rate, one day we will ___ of it.
extra.why: 'Run out of' something means use all of it, so there is none left.

extra.q: Many countries want to reduce their dependence ___ oil and gas.
extra.why: We say 'dependence on' something, just as we say 'depend on' it.

extra.q: Read the paragraph: 'Electric cars do not release fumes into city streets, which helps to keep the air clean. However, they are only as clean as the electricity they use. If that electricity comes from burning coal or gas, the cars are still responsible for some emissions.' Which heading fits best?
opts: Electric cars: cleaner, but not perfect
How to charge an electric car
Why coal is cheaper than gas
The history of the motor car
extra.why: The paragraph gives one good point and one problem, so the best heading shows both sides.

extra.q: Our school council decided to ___ action to save energy.
extra.why: 'Take action' is a fixed phrase that means do something to deal with a problem.

sents: Solar power has several advantages over fossil fuels.
Firstly, sunlight is free and will never run out.
Secondly, solar panels produce no greenhouse gases while they are working.
However, they cannot generate electricity at night, so some of the energy has to be stored in batteries.
Despite this drawback, solar power is likely to play a major role in the future.
There are several simple ways in which families can reduce the energy they use at home.
One of the easiest is to switch off lights and devices when nobody is using them.
Another is to improve the insulation in the roof and walls, so that less heat escapes.
Although this costs money at first, it lowers heating bills for many years.
If every household made these changes, the total savings would be enormous.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'Lots of countries are using way more wind power now.'?
opts: Many countries have significantly increased their use of wind power.
Loads of countries use wind power a lot more now.
Wind power is used by countries, which is good.
Countries are doing wind power more and more, basically.
writing.why: 'Significantly increased' is precise and formal. 'Loads of', 'basically' and 'doing wind power' are chatty, and 'which is good' is vague.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'For instance, many cities now have bike-sharing schemes and electric buses. Some have also created low-emission zones, where the most polluting vehicles must pay to enter.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Cities around the world are finding new ways to cut traffic emissions.
Bicycles were invented in the nineteenth century.
Electric buses are quieter than diesel buses.
Cities are big places where lots of people live.
writing.why: 'For instance' shows that examples of a general point follow. Only the first option is a general point that every example supports.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people believe that individuals can do little to fight climate change, and that only governments and large companies can make a difference. To what extent do you agree or disagree?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: While governments and companies have the greatest power, I disagree that individuals can do little, because millions of small changes add up.
Climate change is a big problem in the world today.
Governments, companies and people are all different.
I think recycling is fun and everyone should try it!
writing.why: The best thesis takes a clear position on the question and gives a reason. The others state facts, say nothing, or are chatty and off the point.

units.title: How we communicate

words.def: a movement of your hand, head or face that shows a meaning
words.ex: Waving goodbye is a ___ that people understand in many countries.

words.def: the way your face, hands and position show how you feel
words.ex: His ___ showed he was nervous: he kept looking at the floor.

words.def: able to speak a language easily and well
words.ex: After five years in Spain, my cousin became ___ in Spanish.

words.def: to understand something in the wrong way
words.ex: Short text messages are easy to ___ because you cannot hear the tone of voice.

words.def: to make someone agree to do something by giving good reasons
words.ex: I tried to ___ my parents to let me have a pet rabbit.

words.def: to show a feeling or an idea in words, pictures or actions
words.ex: Some children find it easier to ___ their feelings through drawing.

words.def: a sound, light, movement or radio wave that carries a message
words.ex: Up in the mountains, my phone had no ___, so I couldn't call home.

words.def: to stop someone while they are speaking by saying something yourself
words.ex: It's rude to ___ someone when they are in the middle of a story.

words.def: the way people from a particular place pronounce words
words.ex: My cousin from Glasgow has a strong Scottish ___.

words.def: to change words from one language into another
words.ex: Can you ___ this menu from French into English?

words.def: the people who watch or listen to a show, film or talk
words.ex: The ___ clapped loudly at the end of her speech.

words.def: looking straight into someone's eyes while you talk to them
words.ex: Good speakers make ___ with the people who are listening.

words.def: to make the sound of a word or a letter in a particular way
words.ex: Many learners find it hard to ___ the 'th' sound in English.

words.def: able to speak two languages equally well
words.ex: My cousin is ___: she speaks Welsh at school and English at home.

words.def: someone who has spoken a language since they were a baby
words.ex: Even a ___ of English sometimes needs to look up a word in a dictionary.

words.def: the way a voice sounds, which shows how the speaker feels
words.ex: I could tell from her ___ of voice that she was annoyed.

words.def: to give only the most important points of something, in a few words
words.ex: Can you ___ the main ideas of the article in three sentences?

words.def: to make something easier to understand by explaining it in more detail
words.ex: Could you ___ what you mean by that, please?

words.def: a way of talking that uses movements of the hands instead of spoken words
words.ex: Our teacher taught us how to say 'thank you' in ___.

words.def: to move your head up and down, often to show that you agree
words.ex: If you agree with me, just ___ your head.

grammar.q: She asked me where ___.
grammar.why: In a reported question, use normal sentence order (I lived), not question order (did I live).

grammar.q: Tom asked ___ I could speak French.
grammar.why: To report a yes/no question, use 'if' (or 'whether').

grammar.q: The teacher told us ___ our phones off during the talk.
grammar.why: To report an order, use tell + person + to + verb: told us to turn.

grammar.q: My friend ___ me to practise speaking English every day.
grammar.why: 'Advise' can be followed by a person + to + verb. We can't say 'suggested me to', 'said me to' or 'explained me to'.

grammar.q: Samuel Morse, ___ gave his name to Morse code, was also a painter.
grammar.why: For a person in a non-defining clause (between commas), use 'who'. 'That' can't be used after a comma like this.

grammar.q: The first text message ___ in 1992.
grammar.why: 1992 is a finished time in the past, so use the past simple passive: was sent.

grammar.q: 'I met your teacher yesterday,' said Mum. Mum told me that she ___ my teacher the day before.
grammar.why: In reported speech, the past simple (met) often moves back to the past perfect: had met.

grammar.q: I wish I ___ Japanese. Then I could chat to my pen friend in her own language.
grammar.why: To wish that the present were different, use a past form after 'wish': I wish I spoke.

grammar.q: You ___ told me you were coming! I would have made more food.
grammar.why: 'Should have' + past participle means it was a good idea, but it didn't happen: you didn't tell me.

grammar.q: Louis Braille, ___ alphabet of raised dots is used by blind people around the world, was born in France.
grammar.why: 'Whose' shows that something belongs to someone: Braille's alphabet. It works in a clause between commas, too.

sentences: She asked me whether I had ever been to Japan.
The teacher told us not to interrupt each other.
My message, which I sent to the wrong person, was very embarrassing.
Do you know how many languages are spoken in India?
You should have told me that you were coming.
Louis Braille invented an alphabet that blind people can read with their fingers.

reading.title: The island where people whistle
reading.text:
On La Gomera, one of Spain's Canary Islands, some people can hold a conversation without saying a single word. Instead, they whistle. Their language, Silbo Gomero, turns Spanish into whistled sounds that rise and fall in pitch.

The island is covered with deep valleys and steep hills, so walking from one farm to the next could take hours. A loud whistle, however, can cross a valley in seconds and be heard several kilometres away. For centuries, shepherds and farmers used Silbo to send messages, warn their neighbours and arrange to meet.

In the twentieth century, roads and telephones arrived, and fewer young people learnt to whistle. The language might have disappeared completely if the island had not decided to protect it. In 1999, Silbo became a compulsory subject in local schools, and today children on the island learn it in class. In 2009, UNESCO recognised it as an important part of the world's cultural heritage.

Scientists find Silbo fascinating, too. Studies have shown that skilled whistlers use the same parts of the brain that normally deal with speech. This suggests that the brain treats whistling as a real language, not just as music.

qs.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: a whistled language and how it was saved

qs.q: Silbo Gomero is based on the Spanish language.
Children on La Gomera can choose whether or not to learn Silbo at school.
It takes most people about a year to learn Silbo well.
What did the brain studies suggest?
opts: The brain treats Silbo like a real language.
Whistling is just a kind of music.
Whistlers have bigger brains than other people.
Silbo is harder to learn than Spanish.

reading.title: Small pictures, big messages
reading.text:
In 1999, a Japanese designer called Shigetaka Kurita was working for a mobile phone company. At that time, text messages had to be very short, and words alone could sound cold or unclear. Kurita's answer was a set of 176 tiny pictures, each one just 12 dots wide and 12 dots high. They became known as emoji.

Many people assume that the word comes from 'emotion', but it does not. It combines two Japanese words: 'e', which means picture, and 'moji', which means character.

At first, emoji were only available in Japan. However, in 2010 they were added to the international system that computers use to display text, and soon smartphones everywhere had them. Today there are more than 3,000, from food and animals to flags and faces.

Emoji do an important job. In a face-to-face conversation, our tone of voice and body language show how we feel. In a written message, these clues are missing, so a short reply such as 'OK' can easily be misunderstood. Adding a smiling face shows that the writer is friendly rather than annoyed.

Kurita's original designs are now so famous that in 2016 they became part of the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the text?
opts: Emoji began in Japan and help to make written messages clearer.
Emoji are more popular in Japan than anywhere else.
Text messages should always be very short.
Museums should collect more mobile phones.

qs.q: The word 'emoji' comes from the English word 'emotion'.
Kurita's first set contained fewer than 200 pictures.
Older people use emoji less often than younger people.
According to the text, why can a reply such as 'OK' be misunderstood?
opts: The reader cannot hear the writer's tone of voice.

extra.q: The party was meant to be a surprise, but my little brother ___.
opts: let the cat out of the bag
hit the nail on the head
extra.why: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means tell a secret by mistake.

extra.q: The line was so bad that I couldn't ___ what she was saying.
extra.why: 'Make out' means manage to hear, see or understand something with difficulty.

extra.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a teacher for help?
opts: Could you possibly explain this again, please?
You need to explain this again.
extra.why: 'Could you possibly... please?' is polite and indirect. The others sound like orders or are rude.

extra.q: Our head teacher ___ a speech at the end-of-year assembly.
extra.why: We 'give a speech' (or 'make a speech'). We don't 'do', 'say' or 'tell' a speech.

extra.q: Her ___ in three languages helped her to get the job. (fluent)
extra.why: After 'Her' we need a noun: fluency.

extra.q: Which sentence best continues the text? 'Humans are not the only animals that communicate with sound. ___'
opts: Whales, for example, make sounds that can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater.
In contrast, many people enjoy music.
extra.why: 'For example' introduces an example that supports the sentence before it.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'I couldn't get my message across'?
opts: I couldn't make people understand what I meant.
I couldn't send my message on time.
I couldn't cross the road to talk to them.
I didn't want to share my message.
extra.why: 'Get a message across' means make people understand it.

extra.q: ___ he had lived in France for years, he still found some French jokes hard to understand.
extra.why: 'Although' is followed by a full clause and shows a surprising contrast. 'Despite' would need a noun or an -ing form.

extra.q: He is very good ___ explaining difficult ideas in simple words.
extra.why: We say 'good at' a skill or an activity. 'Good for' means healthy or useful.

extra.q: Read the paragraph: 'Long before telephones, people found clever ways to send messages over long distances. Some lit fires on hilltops, while others used drums or smoke signals. Sailors raised coloured flags to talk to other ships. All of these methods let news travel faster than a person could walk.' Which heading fits best?
opts: Early ways of sending messages far
How to light a fire on a hill
extra.why: Fires, drums and flags are all examples of one idea: old ways of sending messages over long distances.

sents: Body language often says as much as the words we use.
For example, people who are nervous may avoid eye contact or cross their arms.
In contrast, confident speakers usually stand up straight and smile at their audience.
Listeners notice these signals, often without realising it.
Therefore, anyone giving a presentation should think about how they move as well as what they say.
Learning a second language brings many benefits.
The most obvious one is that it allows you to communicate with more people.
In addition, it can help you to understand another culture, including its jokes and traditions.
This kind of understanding can make travelling abroad far more enjoyable.
For these reasons, many schools encourage pupils to start a new language at a young age.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'Texting has changed how people talk to each other a lot.'?
opts: Text messaging has had a significant impact on the way people communicate.
People text, and talking is different, I guess.
writing.why: 'Had a significant impact on the way people communicate' is precise and formal. 'Loads', 'stuff' and 'I guess' are chatty and vague.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'In Japan, bowing is a common way to say hello. In many parts of Europe, however, friends often kiss each other on the cheek, while a handshake is more usual in business.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: People in different countries greet each other in different ways.
Business meetings can be very long.
writing.why: The paragraph compares greetings in several places, so the topic sentence must cover greetings around the world. The others are too narrow, off topic or vague.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people think children should start learning a foreign language at primary school. Others think it is better to start at secondary school. Discuss both views and give your opinion.' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: Although older pupils may learn grammar faster, I believe children should start at primary school, when they pick up new sounds more easily.
Foreign languages are taught in many schools.
Primary school and secondary school are both important.
Learning languages is, like, really useful for holidays!
writing.why: The best thesis mentions both views and gives a clear opinion with a reason. The others give a fact, avoid the question or are too chatty.

units.title: Science and discovery

words.def: an idea that scientists test to find out whether it is true
words.ex: Her ___ was that plants grow faster with music, so she tested it.

words.def: facts or signs that show that something is true
words.ex: Fossils give us ___ that dinosaurs once lived here.

words.def: an important discovery that solves a problem or opens a new way forward
words.ex: The first vaccine was a major ___ in medicine.

words.def: to study something in detail to understand or explain it
words.ex: Back at the lab, the scientists will ___ the rock samples.

words.def: a room or building where scientists do experiments
words.ex: The ___ was full of test tubes and microscopes.

words.def: by chance, without planning to
words.ex: Fleming ___ discovered penicillin when mould grew on one of his dishes.

words.def: to watch something carefully to learn about it
words.ex: Galileo used a telescope to ___ the moons of Jupiter.

words.def: an idea or set of ideas that explains why something happens
words.ex: Darwin's ___ of evolution changed how we understand living things.

words.def: a group of animals or plants of the same type
words.ex: Scientists discover thousands of new ___ of insects every year.

words.def: what you decide is true after looking at all the facts
words.ex: After the experiment, we wrote our ___ at the bottom of the page.

words.def: to try to find out all the facts about something
words.ex: The team will ___ how dolphins use sounds to find food.

words.def: wanting to know or learn about something
words.ex: Young children are naturally ___ and ask lots of questions.

words.def: facts and numbers that are collected so that they can be studied
words.ex: The weather station collects ___ on rain, wind and temperature every hour.

words.def: a particular way of doing something
words.ex: Scientists must describe their ___ so that others can repeat the experiment.

words.def: a small amount of something that is tested or examined
words.ex: The astronauts brought back a ___ of rock from the Moon.

words.def: to organise and do something, such as an experiment or a survey
words.ex: Our class will ___ a survey about how pupils travel to school.

words.def: to show that something is true by giving facts
words.ex: On the Moon, an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather to ___ that they fall at the same speed.

words.def: to show something that was hidden or not known before
words.ex: Photos from the new telescope ___ galaxies that nobody has ever seen before.

words.def: one of the first people to do something new or to develop a new area of knowledge
words.ex: Marie Curie was a ___ in the study of radioactivity.

words.def: to mix completely with a liquid and disappear into it
words.ex: If you stir the tea, the sugar will ___ more quickly.

grammar.q: If Fleming had cleaned his dishes before his holiday, he ___ penicillin.
grammar.why: In the third conditional, the result uses would/might + have + past participle.

grammar.q: These footprints are 70 million years old. The dinosaur that made them ___ very heavy.
grammar.why: 'Must have been' shows we are sure about something in the past because of the evidence.

grammar.q: You ___ your results before you wrote your conclusion. Now it is full of mistakes.
grammar.why: 'Should have' + past participle means it was a good idea, but you didn't do it.

grammar.q: Penicillin, ___ was discovered in 1928, has saved millions of lives.
grammar.why: Use 'which' for a thing in a non-defining clause (between commas). 'That' is not used after a comma.

grammar.q: Marie Curie, ___ work on radioactivity earned her two Nobel Prizes, was born in Poland.
grammar.why: 'Whose' shows that something belongs to someone: her work.

grammar.q: The rock samples ___ in the laboratory at the moment.
grammar.why: Someone is testing the samples right now, so use the present continuous passive: are being tested.

grammar.q: The results ___ checked more carefully before they were published.
grammar.why: The results didn't check themselves, so use a modal perfect in the passive: should + have been + past participle.

grammar.q: The journalist asked the scientist what ___ next.
grammar.why: In a reported question, use normal word order (she would study), not question order, and move 'will' back to 'would'.

grammar.q: Cambridge, ___ Isaac Newton studied, has one of the oldest universities in the world.
grammar.why: Use 'where' for a place in a non-defining clause when a full clause follows (Newton studied there).

grammar.q: My little brother is so curious! I wish he ___ stop asking 'Why?' all the time.
grammar.why: Use 'wish' + would to complain about something annoying that someone keeps doing.

sentences: Scientists must have made a mistake in their calculations.
The results of the experiment have been checked by three scientists.
Do you know who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter?
I should have asked my teacher for help.
The results should have been checked more carefully.
Ada Lovelace was a pioneer of computer programming.

reading.title: The mould that changed medicine
reading.text:
In September 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his laboratory in London after a summer holiday. Before leaving, he had stacked several dishes of bacteria on a bench. When he examined them, he noticed something unusual. A blue-green mould had grown on one dish, and around it there was a clear ring where the bacteria had been killed.

Fleming was curious rather than annoyed. He grew more of the mould and found that it produced a substance that could destroy many harmful bacteria. He named it penicillin. However, he struggled to produce it in large amounts, and for about ten years his discovery received little attention.

The breakthrough came at the University of Oxford, where a team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain found a way to purify penicillin. In 1941, they tested it on patients, and the results were remarkable. By the mid-1940s, penicillin was being produced in huge quantities, and in 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize.

Fleming's story is often told as a lucky accident, and luck certainly played a part. But the mould only mattered because a scientist was paying attention. Many people might have thrown the dish away without a second thought.

qs.q: What is the main point of the last paragraph?
opts: Luck alone does not explain the discovery.
Fleming was the luckiest scientist in history.
Scientists should never throw dishes away.
The Oxford team deserved more credit than Fleming.

qs.q: Fleming noticed the mould while he was on holiday.
Fleming found it difficult to make large quantities of penicillin.
Florey and Chain had worked with Fleming before 1928.
What did the Oxford team achieve?
opts: They found a way to purify penicillin.
They won the Nobel Prize without Fleming.
They proved that the mould was harmful.

reading.title: The fossil hunter of Lyme Regis
reading.text:
Two hundred years ago, the cliffs near Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England, were an exciting place for collectors. Every winter, storms washed away parts of the cliffs and uncovered the remains of creatures that had lived millions of years earlier.

Mary Anning, who was born in the town in 1799, spent much of her childhood searching these beaches. Her family was poor, and they sold the fossils they found to visitors. When Mary was about twelve, she and her brother discovered the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile that looked a little like a dolphin. Later, she found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, an animal with a long neck and four large flippers.

These finds were important evidence that some species had died out long ago, an idea that many people at the time found hard to accept. Famous scientists travelled to Lyme Regis to ask Mary's opinion. However, because she was a woman, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, and her discoveries were often described by men who took the credit.

Today, Mary Anning is recognised as a pioneer of science. In 2022, a statue of her was unveiled in her home town.

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: to tell the story of an important fossil hunter
to warn readers about storms on the coast
to explain how fossils are formed
to describe the town of Lyme Regis today

qs.q: Mary Anning's family earned money from fossils.
Mary Anning was a member of the Geological Society of London.
Mary Anning wrote several books about her discoveries.
Why were Mary's finds important?
opts: They showed that some animals had died out long ago.
They proved that dolphins are reptiles.
They turned Lyme Regis into a big city.
They were the first fossils ever found.

extra.q: Before the trip, the class ___ some research on the island's birds.
extra.why: We say 'do research' (or 'carry out research'), not 'make research'.

extra.q: Her careful ___ of the data showed a clear pattern. (analyse)
extra.why: After 'Her careful' we need a noun: analysis.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The results were not what the team had expected'?
opts: The team was surprised by the results.
The team knew what the results would be.
The team did not carry out the experiment.
extra.why: If the results were not what they expected, the results surprised them.

extra.q: Some scientists work in laboratories, ___ others spend most of their time outdoors.
extra.why: 'Whereas' compares two different facts or groups of people.

extra.q: Marie Curie is famous ___ her research on radioactivity.
extra.why: We say 'famous for' something.

extra.q: Read the paragraph: 'Many great discoveries began with a simple question. Isaac Newton is said to have wondered why apples fall straight down. Charles Darwin asked why birds on different islands had different beaks. Their curiosity led to ideas that changed science.' Which heading fits best?
extra.why: The paragraph uses two examples to make one point: asking questions leads to discoveries.

extra.q: Which sentence is the most suitable for a science report?
opts: The temperature of the water was measured every ten minutes.
We checked how hot the water was loads of times.
The water got really hot, which was so cool!
Basically, we just kept looking at the water.
extra.why: Science reports are formal and precise. They often use the passive and avoid chatty words like 'loads of' and 'basically'.

extra.q: Which sentence best fills the gap? 'First, we filled three glasses with water at different temperatures. ___ Finally, we timed how long the sugar took to dissolve in each one.'
opts: Next, we added a spoonful of sugar to each glass.
Sugar is bad for your teeth.
In conclusion, the experiment was fun.
extra.why: 'First', 'Next' and 'Finally' show the order of the steps. The missing step comes between filling the glasses and timing the sugar.

extra.q: The scientists ___ an experiment to test their hypothesis.
extra.why: 'Carry out' an experiment means do it. 'Put out' a fire means stop it burning.

extra.q: Scientists have ___ great progress in understanding how the brain works.
extra.why: We say 'make progress', not 'do progress'.

sents: Scientists usually follow a series of steps when they investigate a question.
First, they suggest a hypothesis, which is an idea that can be tested.
Next, they design an experiment and carefully collect data.
After analysing the results, they decide whether the data supports their hypothesis.
Finally, they share their findings so that other scientists can check them.
The invention of the telescope completely changed our understanding of space.
In 1610, Galileo used one to discover four moons travelling around Jupiter.
This was important evidence that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.
As telescopes became more powerful, astronomers found new planets, such as Uranus and Neptune.
Today, space telescopes reveal galaxies that are billions of light years away.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'The scientists did a test and found out some stuff.'?
opts: The scientists conducted an experiment and made an important discovery.
The scientists did a test and found out loads.
The scientists did something and found things.
writing.why: 'Conducted an experiment' and 'made an important discovery' are precise. 'Loads', 'things', 'basically' and 'stuff' are vague or chatty.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'Penicillin was found after mould grew on a dish that had been left out by mistake. Similarly, the microwave oven was invented after an engineer noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Some important discoveries have happened partly by accident.
Chocolate melts easily in warm places.
Penicillin is a kind of medicine.
Science is really hard, to be honest.
writing.why: Both examples are discoveries that began with an accident, so the topic sentence must say this. The others are off topic, too narrow or chatty.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people think that money spent on scientific research is wasted unless it leads to practical results. To what extent do you agree or disagree?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I strongly disagree, because many practical inventions began with research that seemed to have no immediate use.
Scientists work in laboratories and wear white coats.
Research is a thing that costs money.
There are many types of science, such as biology and chemistry.
writing.why: The best thesis gives a clear position and a reason. The others describe science but do not answer the question.

units.title: Cities of the future

words.def: connected with towns and cities
words.ex: More than half of the world's people now live in ___ areas.

words.def: cheap enough for most people to pay for
words.ex: Young families need ___ homes near good schools.

words.def: the basic systems a place needs, such as roads, railways, water pipes and power lines
words.ex: The town needs better ___ before thousands of new homes are built.

words.def: a situation in which there is too much traffic on the roads
words.ex: Road ___ is worst in the morning, when everyone drives to work.

words.def: a person who is walking in the street, not driving or riding
words.ex: The square is closed to cars, so every ___ can walk safely.

words.def: to travel regularly between your home and your work or school
words.ex: My mum has to ___ for an hour to get to her office.

words.def: a very tall building in a city
words.ex: From the top of the ___, the cars below looked like toys.

words.def: a person who lives in a particular place
words.ex: Every ___ of our street was invited to the meeting about the new park.

words.def: going straight up, not across
words.ex: A ___ farm grows vegetables on many floors inside a building.

words.def: with too many people in one place
words.ex: The train was so ___ that we had to stand all the way.

words.def: able to move without a person controlling it
words.ex: In some cities, ___ trains already carry passengers.

words.def: an area of grass, trees or plants in a town, such as a park
words.ex: The new estate has plenty of ___ where children can play.

words.def: buses, trains and trams that everyone can pay to use
words.ex: Many teenagers use ___ to get to school because they are too young to drive.

words.def: the number of people who live in a place
words.ex: The ___ of the world is now more than eight billion.

words.def: an area where people live on the edge of a city, away from the centre
words.ex: We live in a quiet ___ and take the train into the city centre.

words.def: the area around your home, and the people who live in it
words.ex: Our ___ has a library, a park and lots of small shops.

words.def: buildings for people to live in, such as homes and flats
words.ex: The city needs more affordable ___ for young families.

words.def: to knock down a building completely
words.ex: They had to ___ the old factory because it was no longer safe.

words.def: buildings, rooms or equipment that are provided for a particular use
words.ex: The new leisure centre has excellent ___, including two pools and a climbing wall.

words.def: to change something completely, usually to make it better
words.ex: Trees and flowers could ___ this grey street into a lovely place to walk.

grammar.q: We're ___ solar panels fitted on our roof next week.
grammar.why: 'Have something done' means another person does the job for you: we're having panels fitted.

grammar.q: The city council had the old bridge ___ last year.
grammar.why: In 'have something done', the verb is a past participle: had the bridge repaired.

grammar.q: In the future, many cars ___ by computers instead of people.
grammar.why: Computers will do the driving, so use the future passive: will be + past participle (will be driven).

grammar.q: I wish there ___ less traffic outside my school.
grammar.why: After 'wish' about the present, use a past form: I wish there were.

grammar.q: If only they ___ more parks when they built the city!
grammar.why: For a regret about the past, use 'if only' + had + past participle.

grammar.q: ___ the city is very crowded, it has lots of green spaces.
grammar.why: 'Although' is followed by a full clause (the city is crowded). 'Despite' and 'because of' need a noun.

grammar.q: We got our flat ___ before we moved in.
grammar.why: 'Get something done' is like 'have something done': someone else did the job. Use the past participle: painted.

grammar.q: The old car park ___ next year to make room for a playground.
grammar.why: It will happen in the future, and the car park doesn't demolish anything, so use the passive: is going to be demolished.

grammar.q: Many people now work from home, ___ means there is less traffic in the rush hour.
grammar.why: After a comma, 'which' can refer back to a whole idea. 'That' and 'what' cannot be used like this.

grammar.q: If the city ___ the new tram line, the traffic would have got even worse.
grammar.why: Third conditional: if + had (not) + past participle, then would have + past participle.

sentences: We had our bikes checked at the shop.
Vegetables can be grown on the roofs of buildings.
I wish more people would cycle to work.
Do you think driverless cars will make our roads safer?
The old car park is going to be turned into a playground.
Good public transport means that fewer people need to drive.

reading.title: A city in a garden
reading.text:
Imagine a city where giant metal trees light up at night and tall buildings are covered in plants. This is not science fiction: it is Singapore, one of the most crowded places on Earth.

Singapore is a small island with millions of residents, so there is very little room to spread out. Instead of losing its nature, however, the city decided to grow upwards. Many skyscrapers now have gardens on their roofs or plants climbing up their walls. These green walls do more than look attractive. They help to keep the buildings cool, which means less electricity is needed for air conditioning.

The most famous example is Gardens by the Bay, which opened in 2012. Its 18 'Supertrees' are between 25 and 50 metres tall and are covered in thousands of living plants. Some of them have solar panels on top, and they also collect rainwater for the gardens. In the evening, visitors can walk along a high bridge between some of the trees and enjoy a show of light and music.

Planners in other countries are studying Singapore's ideas carefully. Although every city is different, many of them face the same problem: how to make room for more people without losing the green spaces that keep residents healthy and happy.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the text?
opts: Singapore has found ways to keep nature in a crowded city.
Singapore has the tallest trees in the world.
Skyscrapers are bad for the environment.
Solar panels work best on trees.

qs.q: Singapore has plenty of empty land for new buildings.
Plants on buildings can reduce the need for air conditioning.
Most visitors to Gardens by the Bay come from other countries.
What do some of the Supertrees collect?

reading.title: Buses that work like trains
reading.text:
In the 1970s, the Brazilian city of Curitiba had a problem that many growing cities face today. Its population was rising fast, and its roads were becoming more and more crowded. An underground railway was one possible answer, but it would have cost far more than the city could afford.

The city's mayor, an architect called Jaime Lerner, chose a different approach. Instead of digging tunnels, Curitiba gave its buses their own lanes along the main roads, separated from cars and lorries. Because the buses were no longer stuck in traffic jams, they could run quickly and keep to their timetables, just like trains. The first of these routes opened in 1974.

Later, the city added something that became famous around the world: glass 'tube' stations. Passengers pay when they enter the tube, not when they get on the bus. The platform is at the same height as the bus floor, so passengers can step straight on board, and wheelchairs and pushchairs can roll on easily. Some of the longest buses can carry more than 200 passengers.

The idea, now known as bus rapid transit, was copied by Bogotá in Colombia and by many other cities. Today, more than 150 cities around the world have similar systems. Curitiba showed that a city does not always need the most expensive solution. Sometimes a clever idea is enough.

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: to show how a city solved its transport problem with a cheaper idea
to describe the history of Brazil
to explain how an underground railway is built
to persuade readers to stop travelling by car

qs.q: Curitiba decided against an underground railway mainly because of the cost.
In Curitiba's system, passengers buy their tickets from the bus driver.
Most people in Curitiba travel to work by bus.
Why can wheelchairs roll onto the buses easily?
opts: The platform is level with the floor of the bus.
The drivers lift them on board.
The buses stop on the pavement.

extra.q: The roads are busiest during ___ hour, when people travel to and from work.
extra.why: 'Rush hour' is the fixed phrase for the busy time when people travel to and from work.

extra.q: Big cities offer many jobs. ___, housing there is often very expensive.
extra.why: 'However' introduces a contrast: a good point followed by a problem.

extra.q: Thousands of ___ travel into London by train every morning. (commute)
extra.why: After 'Thousands of' we need a plural noun for people: commuters.

extra.q: Which sentence is the most suitable for a report to the city council?
opts: Traffic congestion in the city centre has increased considerably.
The traffic in town is totally crazy these days.
There are way too many cars around now.
Honestly, driving in town is a nightmare!
extra.why: A formal report uses precise words like 'congestion' and 'considerably' and avoids chatty language.

extra.q: Which sentence best fills the gap? 'Cities are growing fast. ___ This means that planners must find new ways to provide homes and transport.'
opts: By 2050, about two thirds of people may live in urban areas.
My uncle lives in a city.
Buses and trains are types of transport.
extra.why: The missing sentence must give a fact about growth, so that 'This means...' follows logically.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The new park is within walking distance of most homes'?
opts: Most people can easily walk to the new park.
Most people need a car to reach the new park.
The new park is inside most people's homes.
Walking is not allowed in the new park.
extra.why: 'Within walking distance' means close enough to walk to.

extra.q: The old cinema was ___ to make space for a new library.
extra.why: 'Pull down' a building means destroy it. 'Put up' a building means build it.

extra.q: Our flat is close ___ the station, so I can walk there in five minutes.
extra.why: We say 'close to' a place (or 'near' a place).

extra.q: Read the paragraph: 'In many cities, flat roofs are being turned into small farms. Residents grow tomatoes, herbs and salad leaves just metres above the busy streets. The plants also help to keep the buildings cool, and the gardens give neighbours a place to meet.' Which heading fits best?
extra.why: Every sentence is about growing food on city roofs and the good things it brings.

extra.q: The council plans to ___ the city's old railway station. (modern)
extra.why: After 'plans to' we need a verb. 'Modernise' means make something more modern.

sents: Traffic congestion is a serious problem in many large cities.
It wastes people's time and makes the air dirtier.
One solution is to improve public transport, so that fewer people need to drive.
Another is to build safe cycle lanes, which encourage more people to travel by bike.
If cities combine both measures, their streets could become quieter, cleaner and safer.
Parks and other green spaces bring many benefits to city residents.
Above all, they give people a place to relax, exercise and meet their neighbours.
Trees also provide shade, which keeps streets cooler on hot days.
Their roots and the soil around them soak up rainwater, which can reduce flooding.
For these reasons, planners should include green spaces in every new neighbourhood.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'The city got a lot bigger over the last few years.'?
opts: The city has grown rapidly in recent years.
The city got loads bigger lately.
The city changed in size, sort of.
The city is big now and it wasn't before.
writing.why: 'Has grown rapidly in recent years' is short and precise. 'Loads', 'lately' and 'sort of' are chatty, and the last option is clumsy.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'Sensors can show drivers where the nearest free parking space is. Street lights can dim themselves automatically when nobody is around, which saves energy.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Technology is helping cities to run more efficiently.
Driving in cities is very stressful.
Street lights were first used hundreds of years ago.
writing.why: Both sentences are examples of technology making a city work better. The others are off topic or too chatty.

writing.q: Essay question: 'In many cities, more and more people live in tall apartment buildings. Is this a positive or a negative development?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I believe tall apartment buildings are mainly positive, because they house many people while leaving more land for parks.
Some buildings in cities are very tall.
My cousin lives on the tenth floor of a building.
Tall buildings are both positive and negative, and there are lots of things to say.
writing.why: The best thesis gives a clear answer and a reason. The others state a fact, tell a story or stay vague.

units.title: Sport and teamwork

words.def: a person who is in the same team as you
words.ex: She passed the ball to a ___, who scored the winning goal.

words.def: the person or team that you play against
words.ex: At the end of the match, she shook hands with her ___.

words.def: to work together with other people to reach the same goal
words.ex: In a rowing race, all eight rowers must ___ perfectly to move the boat fast.

words.def: plans for how to win a game or reach a goal
words.ex: At half-time, the coach changed the team's ___.

words.def: the person who makes sure players follow the rules in a match
words.ex: The ___ blew the whistle to start the second half.

words.def: the quality of not giving up, even when something is difficult
words.ex: With hard work and ___, she finally won the race.

words.def: the physical energy to keep going for a long time
words.ex: Marathon runners need great ___ to run for 42 kilometres.

words.def: harm done to a person's body, for example in an accident or a game
words.ex: He missed three matches because of a knee ___.

words.def: to make someone want to do something and work hard at it
words.ex: A good captain knows how to ___ the team when they are losing.

words.def: a person who watches a sports event
words.ex: Every ___ in the stadium stood up and cheered.

words.def: to take part in a contest and try to win it
words.ex: Athletes from more than 200 countries ___ at the Olympic Games.

words.def: fair, kind and polite behaviour in sport, even when you lose
words.ex: Helping an opponent who has fallen is a great example of ___.

words.def: a person who trains hard to take part in sports, especially running, jumping and throwing
words.ex: The ___ trained for four years to compete in the Olympic Games.

words.def: a competition in which many players or teams play a series of games to find one winner
words.ex: Sixteen schools took part in the netball ___.

words.def: the act of winning a game or a competition
words.ex: The fans cheered loudly after the team's 2-0 ___.

words.def: a cup or other prize that is given to the winner of a competition
words.ex: The captain lifted the ___ high above her head.

words.def: to win a place in the next stage of a competition by doing well
words.ex: She must run 100 metres in under 12 seconds to ___ for the national championships.

words.def: doing a sport for fun, not as a paid job
words.ex: My uncle plays for an ___ football team on Sunday mornings.

words.def: to do gentle exercise to get your body ready for sport
words.ex: Always ___ for ten minutes before you start running fast.

words.def: connected with the body rather than the mind
words.ex: Rugby is a very ___ sport, so players need to be strong.

grammar.q: If our goalkeeper ___ that penalty, we would have won the cup.
grammar.why: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, then would have + past participle.

grammar.q: I'm not sure why Ella missed training. She ___ ill.
grammar.why: 'Might have been' shows a possibility in the past. We are not sure, so 'must' and 'can't' are too certain.

grammar.q: The coach ___ that we should drink more water during matches.
grammar.why: 'Recommend' can be followed by 'that'. 'Tell' and 'encourage' need a person first (told us, encouraged us).

grammar.q: The stadium ___ for the final, so it looks brand new.
grammar.why: The stadium didn't paint anything, so use the passive. The result is clear now, so use the present perfect passive.

grammar.q: Wembley Stadium, ___ the FA Cup Final is played, can hold 90,000 people.
grammar.why: Use 'where' for a place when a full clause follows (the final is played there).

grammar.q: Despite ___ a goal down at half-time, the team won 3-1.
grammar.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not by a full clause.

grammar.q: I wish I ___ my football boots. I had to play in my trainers!
grammar.why: For a regret about the past, use 'wish' + had + past participle: I wish I had brought.

grammar.q: Our team ___ new shirts designed for the tournament.
grammar.why: 'Have something done': the team didn't design the shirts themselves; someone else did it for them.

grammar.q: The coach promised that she ___ give us extra training before the final.
grammar.why: In reported speech, 'will' usually becomes 'would': 'I will give you...' becomes 'she would give us...'.

grammar.q: They lost 10-0. Their defenders ___ practised very much this week.
grammar.why: 'Can't have' + past participle shows we are almost sure that something did not happen.

sentences: The coach told us to pass the ball more quickly.
Our goalkeeper, whose gloves were too big, kept dropping the ball.
The stadium will be opened by the team captain.
Do you know how many players there are in a rugby team?
I wish I had brought my football boots.
Only the best teams will qualify for the final.

reading.title: Winning together
reading.text:
The Tour de France is one of the toughest races in the world. Every July, about 170 cyclists ride more than 3,000 kilometres around France in three weeks. It may look like a contest between individuals, but no rider could win it alone.

Each team has eight riders, and usually only one of them has a real chance of winning. Most of the others are known as 'domestiques', a French word meaning 'servants'. Their job is to help their leader. They fetch water bottles and food from the team car, ride in front of the leader to block the wind and, if the leader's bike breaks, they may even hand over their own.

Riding just behind another cyclist takes much less effort than riding at the front, because the rider in front pushes through the air. Domestiques take turns at the front so that their leader can save energy for the hardest mountain climbs. By the final week, many of them are exhausted, having spent their strength on someone else's success.

Despite this, domestiques are highly respected by fans and other riders, who know that the race is rarely won by one person. The winner wears the famous yellow jersey in Paris, but the whole team has earned it.

qs.q: Why did the writer write this text?
opts: to show that winning a cycling race depends on a whole team
to explain how to repair a racing bike
to describe the mountains of France
to persuade readers to become professional cyclists

qs.q: Most riders in a team expect to win the Tour de France.
Cycling just behind another rider is easier than cycling at the front.
Domestiques often become team leaders later in their careers.
What does the French word 'domestique' mean?

reading.title: Two seconds of teamwork
reading.text:
In a Formula One race, drivers usually have to stop at least once to change their tyres. These stops take place in the pit lane, and every second counts: a slow stop can cost a driver several places, while a fast one can help them win.

A modern pit stop is one of the most impressive examples of teamwork in sport. Around twenty mechanics surround the car the moment it stops, and each of them has just one job. Two of them lift the car at the front and back. At each wheel, three people work together: one removes the wheel nut, one pulls off the old wheel and one fits the new one. The best teams can change all four wheels in just over two seconds.

Such speed does not happen by chance. Teams practise pit stops hundreds of times during a season, and they study videos to see where they can save a fraction of a second. If one person makes even a tiny mistake, the whole stop is slowed down.

Drivers receive the trophies and most of the attention. However, many of them say that a race is never won by one person alone, but by the whole team.

qs.q: Why did the writer write this text?
opts: to show how teamwork makes very fast pit stops possible
to explain all the rules of Formula One
to persuade readers to become racing drivers
to compare the fastest drivers in history

qs.q: Each mechanic in a pit stop has several different jobs.
Teams watch videos of their pit stops to find ways to be faster.
Pit stop mechanics are paid more than other members of the team.
How many people work on each wheel during a pit stop?

extra.q: We were losing 2-0, but we didn't ___, and in the end we drew 2-2.
opts: cost an arm and a leg
extra.why: 'Throw in the towel' means give up.

extra.q: Our team ___ the match 3-1.
extra.why: You win a match or a game, but you beat a person or a team.

extra.q: The final was ___ until Sunday because of the storm.
extra.why: 'Put off' means move an event to a later time.

extra.q: Swimming is a very ___ sport at our school: everyone wants to win. (compete)
extra.why: We need an adjective after 'very' to describe the sport: competitive.

extra.q: ___ he had a sore ankle, Leo played the whole match.
extra.why: 'Even though' is followed by a full clause (he had a sore ankle). 'Despite' and 'in spite of' need a noun or an -ing form.

extra.q: Which sentence best completes the paragraph? 'Team sports teach children many useful skills. They learn to communicate clearly and to trust others. ___'
opts: They also learn how to deal with losing as well as winning.
However, football was invented in England.
As a result, stadiums are very large.
extra.why: The last sentence adds one more skill, so it continues the same idea with 'also'.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The match was called off because of the snow'?
opts: The match was cancelled because of the snow.
The match was played in the snow.
The match started late because of the snow.
The match was moved to a snowy place.
extra.why: 'Call off' means cancel, so the match did not happen.

extra.q: Which sentence is the most suitable for a formal email to a sports club?
opts: I would like to enquire about joining your junior tennis team.
Hey, can I join your tennis team?
I wanna play tennis with you lot.
extra.why: 'I would like to enquire about...' is polite and formal. 'Hey', 'wanna' and 'you lot' are informal.

extra.q: She was very proud ___ her team's performance in the final.
extra.why: We say 'proud of' someone or something.

extra.q: Read the paragraph: 'Team sports can help children in many ways. They learn to set goals, manage their time and keep going when things are difficult. Playing with others also helps them to make friends and feel part of a group.' Which heading fits best?
extra.why: The first sentence gives the main idea, and the rest lists ways in which team sports help children.

sents: Successful football teams depend on teamwork rather than on one star player.
Even the most talented striker cannot score without good passes from teammates.
Similarly, defenders must cooperate closely to stop the other team from attacking.
This is why coaches spend so much time practising tactics with the whole team.
In the end, a group that plays together will usually beat a group of individuals.
The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896.
At those first Games, fewer than 300 athletes from 14 countries took part.
Since then, the Games have grown into one of the biggest sporting events in the world.
Today, more than 10,000 athletes from over 200 countries compete.
However, the aim is still the same: to bring people together through sport.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'Our team played really badly and lost by loads.'?
opts: Our team performed poorly and suffered a heavy defeat.
Our team was rubbish and lost massively.
Our team did bad and lost by a lot.
Our team played and lost, which was not good.
writing.why: 'Performed poorly' and 'a heavy defeat' are precise. 'Rubbish' and 'massively' are slang, 'did bad' is wrong, and the last option is vague.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'Regular training builds stamina and strength. Just as importantly, playing in a team teaches young people how to cooperate and how to cope with losing.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Playing sport has both physical and social benefits for young people.
Many sports are played with a ball.
Losing a match is never fun.
Sport is awesome and I love it!
writing.why: The paragraph gives one benefit for the body and one for getting on with others, so the topic sentence must mention both. The others are off topic, too narrow or chatty.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people think that professional athletes are paid too much money. Do you agree or disagree?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I agree that top athletes are paid too much, because they earn far more than doctors and nurses, whose work saves lives.
Football players are famous all over the world.
Athletes are paid, and some people think it is too much.
writing.why: The best thesis gives a clear position and a reason. The others are off topic, too vague or only repeat the question.

units.title: Holidays and tourism

words.def: the place that someone is travelling to
words.ex: Spain is the most popular holiday ___ for British tourists.

words.def: a place to stay, such as a hotel, a flat or a campsite
words.ex: The price of the trip includes flights and ___.

words.def: a plan of a journey that shows where you will go and when
words.ex: Our ___ includes three days in Rome and two days in Florence.

words.def: a famous building or place that is easy to recognise
words.ex: The Eiffel Tower is the most famous ___ in Paris.

words.def: the buildings, traditions and history that a country has kept from the past
words.ex: Stonehenge is an important part of Britain's ___.

words.def: a short trip to visit a place, usually as part of a longer holiday
words.ex: On the third day, we went on an ___ to a volcano.

words.def: a holiday in which the travel and the hotel are booked together for one price
words.ex: A ___ is often cheaper than booking flights and hotels separately.

words.def: a person who travels cheaply, carrying their things in a large bag on their back
words.ex: Every ___ in the hostel had a map and a guidebook.

words.def: travel to natural places that tries to protect the environment and help local people
words.ex: In Costa Rica, ___ brings money to villages and helps to protect the rainforest.

words.def: the busiest time of year for travel, when prices are highest
words.ex: Flights cost much more in the ___, when schools are on holiday.

words.def: a tired feeling after a long flight to a place where the time is very different
words.ex: After flying from London to Tokyo, I had terrible ___ for three days.

words.def: an arrangement to keep a room, a table or a seat for you
words.ex: We made a ___ at the restaurant for eight o'clock.

words.def: the act of leaving a place, especially at the start of a journey
words.ex: Please arrive at the airport two hours before ___.

words.def: a place where many people go on holiday, with hotels, beaches or ski slopes
words.ex: The ski ___ was packed with families during the February half-term.

words.def: the natural things you can see in a place, such as mountains, lakes and forests
words.ex: The ___ in the Scottish Highlands is wild and beautiful.

words.def: a confused or upset feeling when you visit a place where life is very different
words.ex: Many students feel ___ when they first move to a new country.

words.def: pretty, especially in an old-fashioned way, like a scene in a painting
words.ex: We stayed in a ___ village with stone cottages and a little harbour.

words.def: extremely beautiful or amazing
words.ex: From the top of the hill, the view was ___.

words.def: still beautiful and natural, without many new buildings or visitors
words.ex: The island has long, ___ beaches with hardly any hotels.

words.def: to walk slowly around a place without a clear plan
words.ex: It's fun to ___ through the narrow streets of an old town.

grammar.q: If we had booked earlier, we ___ a cheaper flight.
grammar.why: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, then would have + past participle (would have got).

grammar.q: I wish we ___ here for another week. The holiday is going too quickly!
grammar.why: To wish that the present were different, use a past form after 'wish': I wish we were staying.

grammar.q: If only we ___ the reviews of the hotel before we booked it!
grammar.why: For a regret about the past, use 'if only' + had + past participle: if only we had checked.

grammar.q: We ___ booked our hotel in advance. Now everything in the town is full.
grammar.why: 'Should have' + past participle means it was a good idea, but we didn't do it.

grammar.q: These days, Machu Picchu ___ by thousands of people every day.
grammar.why: Machu Picchu doesn't visit anyone; people visit it. Use the present simple passive: is visited.

grammar.q: The Eiffel Tower ___ for the World's Fair of 1889.
grammar.why: 1889 is a finished time, and the tower didn't build anything, so use the past simple passive: was built.

grammar.q: We had our photo ___ in front of the Taj Mahal.
grammar.why: 'Have something done': someone else took the photo for us. Use the past participle: taken.

grammar.q: Venice, ___ is famous for its canals, welcomes millions of visitors every year.
grammar.why: Use 'which' for a place or thing in a non-defining clause (between commas) when the verb follows. 'That' is not used after a comma.

grammar.q: The receptionist asked us how long ___.
grammar.why: In a reported question, use normal word order (we were staying), not question order, and move the tense back.

grammar.q: ___ it rained every day, we had a wonderful holiday.
grammar.why: 'Although' is followed by a full clause (it rained every day). 'Despite' and 'in spite of' need a noun or an -ing form.

sentences: The Eiffel Tower was built for the World's Fair of 1889.
We should have booked our hotel in advance.
The receptionist asked us how long we were staying.
I wish we were staying here for another week.
Jet lag can make travellers feel tired for several days.
Have you ever been on a package holiday?

reading.title: The man who invented the package holiday
reading.text:
Today, millions of people buy package holidays, in which the travel and the accommodation are arranged together. The idea goes back to a British cabinet-maker called Thomas Cook.

In 1841, Cook organised a day trip by train for about 500 people from Leicester to a meeting in Loughborough, around 11 miles away. Each passenger paid one shilling, and the price included the train ticket and food for the journey. Railways were still new at the time, and a group trip like this was something completely different.

The trip was such a success that Cook began to organise more. Over the next few years, he took groups to the seaside and to Scotland, and in 1855 he led his first tour across the Channel, to an exhibition in Paris. His customers did not need to plan anything themselves: Cook booked the tickets, arranged where they would stay and often travelled with them as a guide.

In 1872, he led the first organised tour around the world, which lasted more than 200 days. By then, travel was no longer only for the rich. Thanks to cheap train tickets and careful planning, ordinary working families could explore places that their grandparents had only heard about.

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: to explain how one man made organised travel possible for ordinary people
to describe the history of the railway
to persuade readers to buy package holidays
to compare holidays in Leicester and Paris

qs.q: The passengers on the 1841 trip had to pay for their food separately.
Cook's customers did not have to find their own places to stay.
Thomas Cook had travelled abroad many times before 1841.
How long did the first organised tour around the world last?

reading.title: Why jet lag happens
reading.text:
Flying across the world is exciting, but many travellers spend the first days of their holiday feeling tired, hungry at strange times and wide awake in the middle of the night. This is jet lag, and it happens because of the body clock.

Deep inside your brain, a tiny group of cells works like a clock. It tells your body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up, mainly by noticing light and darkness. Normally, it matches the day and night outside. However, if you fly from London to Tokyo, which is eight or nine hours ahead, your body clock is still on British time. When it is morning in Japan, your body thinks it is the middle of the night.

The body clock can only adjust slowly, often by about an hour a day. As a result, recovering from a long flight can take several days. Many people also find that flying east is harder than flying west, because it is easier for the body to stay up later than to go to sleep earlier.

Experts suggest a few ways to adjust more quickly. One of the most effective is to spend time outside in daylight at your destination, as sunlight helps to reset the clock. Eating meals at local times can help too.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the text?
opts: Jet lag happens when the body clock does not match the time in a new place.
Tokyo is a difficult city to visit.
It is impossible to sleep on a plane.

qs.q: The body clock uses light and darkness to decide when you should sleep.
Most people recover from a long flight within a few hours.
Children suffer from jet lag less than adults.
According to the text, what is one of the best ways to adjust?
opts: staying in a dark hotel room

extra.q: We ___ a room at a small hotel near the beach.
extra.why: We 'book a room' (or 'reserve a room'). We don't 'make' or 'do' a room.

extra.q: We ___ early in the morning to catch the first ferry.
extra.why: 'Set off' means start a journey. 'Put off' means move something to a later time.

extra.q: When we arrived at the hotel, we ___ at the reception desk.
extra.why: You 'check in' when you arrive at a hotel and 'check out' when you leave.

extra.q: We arrived ___ Paris late in the evening.
extra.why: We 'arrive in' a city or country, and 'arrive at' a building such as a station or a hotel. We never 'arrive to' a place.

extra.q: Tourism has a huge effect ___ small islands.
extra.why: We say 'an effect on' something, just as we say 'an impact on' it.

extra.q: The hotel was small and quite old. ___, the views from our room were breathtaking.
extra.why: 'However' introduces a contrast: first the bad points, then a good one.

extra.q: Tourism brings great ___ benefits to the region. (economy)
extra.why: 'Economic' means connected with money and jobs in a country. 'Economical' means cheap to use, like an economical car.

extra.q: Which sentence is the most suitable for a formal letter of complaint to a hotel?
opts: I am writing to complain about the condition of my room.
Your hotel was a total disaster, mate.
OMG, the room was so gross!
Just wanted to say the room wasn't great.
extra.why: A formal letter starts politely and clearly: 'I am writing to complain about...'. The others are rude or chatty.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The hotel was fully booked'?
opts: There were no free rooms at the hotel.
The hotel had a lot of books.
The hotel was closed for the winter.
extra.why: 'Fully booked' means that every room has already been reserved.

extra.q: Which sentence best continues the text? 'Tourism can bring problems to popular places. ___'
opts: For example, crowds of visitors can damage old buildings and natural sites.
However, many people enjoy going on holiday.
In conclusion, tourists like taking photos.
Paris is the capital of France.
extra.why: 'For example' introduces a problem that supports the sentence before it. The others change the subject.

sents: Tourism can bring many benefits to a region.
The most important is that it creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and shops.
People with these jobs then spend their wages locally, which helps other businesses too.
In addition, entrance fees paid by tourists can be used to protect historic buildings.
For these reasons, many countries work hard to attract more visitors.
There are several simple ways to be a responsible tourist.
First, try to stay in small, locally owned hotels and eat in local restaurants.
This means that more of your money stays in the community you are visiting.
Second, respect local customs, such as dressing modestly when you visit religious buildings.
Small actions like these help to make tourism good for everyone.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'Loads more people go on holiday abroad than before.'?
opts: The number of people travelling abroad has risen considerably.
Way more people go abroad now.
People go abroad, and there are more of them.
Going abroad is more and more and stuff.
writing.why: 'The number of people... has risen considerably' is precise and formal. 'Way more' and 'stuff' are chatty, and the third option is clumsy.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'For example, crowds of visitors can wear away the paths in national parks. In some popular cities, rents have also risen so much that many local people can no longer afford to live in the centre.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Tourism can cause serious problems for the places that people visit.
National parks are beautiful places to visit.
Rents are very high in many cities.
Holidays are the best, aren't they?
writing.why: 'For example' shows that examples of a general point follow. Both examples are problems caused by tourism. The others are off topic, too narrow or chatty.

writing.q: Essay question: 'International tourism has grown rapidly in recent decades. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: In my view, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, because tourism creates jobs and helps people to understand other cultures.
Tourism has grown a lot in recent decades.
There are advantages and disadvantages to everything in life.
Last summer, I went to Italy with my family.
writing.why: The best thesis answers the question clearly and gives reasons. The others repeat the question, stay vague or tell a story.
